tip: Object pronouns follow the verb and subject: 'gwahododd nhw ni' = they invited us, with 'nhw' the subject and 'ni' the object.
Welsh has no word for 'of'; it just puts nouns side by side. In 'gwlad y gân' (land of the song), 'y' is simply 'the'.
The '-ir' ending marks an action with no named doer: 'cenir' means is sung.
The '-ach' ending makes comparatives, and 'na' means than: 'gynhesach na' means warmer than.
'tri' (three) triggers aspirate mutation: 'peth' becomes 'pheth'. 'tri pheth' means three things.
To negate a definite object, Welsh uses 'mo' plus a pronoun ending: 'mo' + 'hi' becomes 'mohoni' (not her).
Clock times use 'o'r gloch', literally of the bell: 'am wyth o'r gloch' = at eight o'clock. 'am' marks at.
The echo 'hi' shows 'ei' means her, not his: 'ei mam hi' is her mother.
Adjectives soft-mutate after a feminine noun: 'cyntaf' becomes 'gyntaf'. 'y wobr gyntaf' = the first prize.
Nouns stay singular after a number: 'wyth gwestai' is literally eight guest, not guests.
'dysgu' covers both learning and teaching. Here 'dysgais i nofio' means I learned to swim.
'hen' (old) comes before its noun and softens it: 'tŷ' turns into 'hen dŷ'.
'yn' becomes 'yng' before g, and 'gogledd' becomes 'ngogledd': 'yng ngogledd' means in the north of.
'allwch chi ...?' is a polite way to ask can you: 'allwch chi siarad' means can you speak.
Eleven is 'un ar ddeg', literally one on ten, from the older base-twenty counting system.
'i' means to when telling time: 'ugain munud i bedwar' is twenty minutes to four.
'On a day' is shown by a soft mutation, with no word for 'on': 'dydd' becomes 'ddydd'. 'ddydd Sul' = on Sunday.
'can' (hundred) triggers a nasal mutation on the next word: 'blwydd' becomes 'mlwydd'. 'saith can mlwydd oed' = 700 years old.
Use 'mewn' for in a or some (indefinite) and 'yn' for in the (definite): 'mewn tri sir'.
'ei' meaning his soft-mutates the next word: 'dwylo' becomes 'ddwylo'. 'ei ddwylo' = his hands.
The '-wch' ending makes a command to 'chi', formal or group: 'trowch' means turn. Compare 'eisteddwch' (sit down) and 'edrychwch' (look).
'well' is the irregular comparative of 'da' (good). 'na' means than: 'heddiw'n well na ddoe', today is better than yesterday.
Add '-ach' to an adjective for the comparative: 'oer' (cold) becomes 'oerach' (colder). 'na' after it means than.
'fy' (my) triggers nasal mutation: 'taid' (grandfather) becomes 'fy nhaid'. The 't' turns to 'nh'.
Welsh builds tens as a unit plus 'deg' (ten): 'dri deg' is thirty, literally three tens.
Use 'am' for clock times: 'am chwech' means at six. 'am' can also mean for or about.
Placing 'yn' before an adjective makes it describe an action: 'cyflym' (fast) softens to 'gyflym', meaning fast or quickly.
Give age with 'oed' after a number: 'yn ddeg oed' is ten years old, literally ten age.
The 'that' in a reported clause is 'bod', softened to 'fod' here: 'sylwais i fod y drws ar agor'.
Wrap 'our' around the noun for emphasis: 'ein tîm ni' = our team, with 'ni' echoing the possessive 'ein'.
